--- title: "BIOL 220 Introduction" --- ## About me ::: columns ::: {.column width="40%"} **Andy Rominger** he/him, settler/haole ![](/img/ohana.png) ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} **Father, husband** Living and working on **stolen ʻāina** **Assistant Professor** SoLS Started August 2023 Born and raised in New Mexico I studied **biodiversity in Hawaiʻi** during my PhD, left for a few years, back now working on biodiversity and **Indigenous data sovereignty** ::: ::: ## Setting our intentions ::: {style="text-align: center;"} ʻAʻa i ka hula, waiho ka hilahila i ka hale ::: ## Course objectives Students will be able to: - apply statistical knowledge to analyze data and answer biological questions - communicate and report data visually, orally, and in writing - apply their knowledge to areas of personal interest such as conservation, sustainability, and health - identify racist and colonial legacies in biostatistics and ways to positively intervene to stop the perpetuation of those legacies # What is statistics? ## What is statistics? > Statistics is the study of methods to describe, measure, and test hypotheses about nature from samples. Statistics gives us tools to *describe the uncertainty* of measurements and the scientific insights we seek to gain from those measurements. ## What is statistics? Comes down to one question: > Sure? ## Goals of statistics 1. Estimation 2. Hypothesis testing ## Biology is messy Three sources of variation: - Measurement error - Random variation - Complexity Adapted from www.statstree.org ## Biology is messy [Measurement Error]{.alert} - No measurement device is perfect - More precise tools are better - e.g. digital stopwatch versus second-hand on an analog clock ::: {.fragment} [Random variation and error]{.alert} - We can't control everything, there's always *some* random noise - We can't [sample]{.alert} everything - e.g. random temperature fluctuates affect biological processes, finite sample sizes means there's variation between studies ::: ## Biology is messy [Complexity]{.alert} - We can't measure unknown processes - Many environmental, genetic, and other factors affect biology - e.g. a person's environment, genetics could affect drug efficacy ## What are the sources of variation? {.top-align} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.pause-think} Species richness across the Hawaiian islands is highly variable, how could the sources of variation contribute to variability in species richness: **measurement error**, **random variation**, or **complexity**? ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](/img/hi_arth.png){width="65%"} ::: ::: ## What are the sources of variation? {.top-align} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.pause-think} Species richness across the Hawaiian islands is highly variable, how could the sources of variation contribute to variability in species richness: **measurement error**, **random variation**, or **complexity**? ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Answer** - Measurement error (e.g. taxonomic misidentification) is likely small to medium - Random variation is likely large, (e.g. failing to detect everything) - Complexity is huge: How species evolve into new forms and interact to form ecosystems is immensely complex ::: ::: ## Syllabus On Google Classroom # Break! ## Logistics 1. In lab you will be registering for a Koa server account (make sure to do this!) 2. Nothing else due this week :) ## Learning goals 1. Know why and how biologists use statistics 2. Explain variables in your data 3. Randomly sample a population ## 1. Know why and how biologists use statistics ## Learning objectives: - Define statistics as the measurement of uncertainty and pursuit of insights in light of uncertainty - Describe sources of uncertainty - Describe uncertainty in terms of [probability]{.alert} and [distributions]{.alert} - Describe the goals of statistics as [parameter estimation]{.alert} and [hypothesis testing]{.alert} - Formulate parameters to estimate and statistical hypotheses to test - Distinguish between a [population]{.alert} and a [sample]{.alert} - Distinguish between a [parameter]{.alert} and an [estimate]{.alert} ## What is statistics? > Statistics is the study of methods to describe, measure, and test hypotheses about nature from samples. Statistics gives us tools to *quantify the uncertainty* of measurements and the scientific insights we seek to gain from those measurements. ## Goals of statistics 1. Estimation 2. Hypothesis testing ## Estimation > [Estimation]{.alert} is the process of inferring an unknown quantity of a [population]{.alert} using [sample]{.alert} data - [Population]{.alert}: all individual units in a collective (e.g. trees in a forest, cells in a body, genes in a genome, etc.) - [Sample]{.alert}: a subset of the population ## Parameter vs. Estimate > A [parameter]{.alert} is a quantity describing a [population]{.alert}, whereas an [estimate]{.alert} or a [statistic]{.alert} is a related quantity calculated from a sample - [Parameter]{.alert}: the "Truth" about a [population]{.alert} - [Estimate]{.alert} (aka [Statistic]{.alert}): what we calculate from a [sample]{.alert} that represents our best guess of the parameter value ## Parameters ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Parameter type Biological example
average the average mass of a certain bird species
proportion the proportion of fertile seeds in a fruit
variation the variance in leaf area within a tree
relationship the relationship between latitude and species diversity
````` ::: ::: ## [Activity]{.alert}: Body sizes of uhu Look around and find the uhu, measure them (to nearest mm), record the data in google classroom ![](/img/uhu.png){width="65%" fig-align="center"} ## Distinguishing [Samples]{.alert} and [Populations]{.alert} ::: {.pause-think} In the *uhu body size* activity 1. What could the [population]{.alert} be? 2. What could represent a [sample]{.alert}? ::: ## Distinguishing [Estimates]{.alert} and [Parameters]{.alert} ::: {.pause-think} In the *uhu body size* activity 1. What could be a useful [parameter]{.alert} to describe some aspect of the population? 2. What is the [estimate]{.alert} of that parameter? ::: ## Sources of variation [Measurement error]{.alert} - No measurement device is perfect [Random variation and sampling error]{.alert} - We can't control everything, there's always *some* noise [Complexity]{.alert} - We can't measure everything - Many environmental, genetic, and other factors affect biology ## Hypothesis testing A [scientific hypothesis]{.alert} is a proposition about how the world works
A [statistical hypothesis]{.alert} is a specific claim regarding a population parameter.
A [statistical hypothesis]{.alert} is related to but generally more specific than a scientific hypothesis ## Comparing scientific and statistical hypotheses Example: **Uhu body sizes** [Scientific hypotheses]{.alert} are propositions about how the world works > Uhu have gotten smaller in waters around Hawaiʻi due to colonizer (mis)management and ecosystem degradation. [Statistical hypotheses]{.alert} are related, but specific about population parameters > The mean length of the contemporary uhu population is smaller than the historic baseline mean of 550 mm, i.e., $(\mu_\text{now} - \mu_\text{past}) < 0$ ## 2. Explain variables in your data **Learning goals:** - Define [variable]{.alert} - Distinguish [categorical]{.alert}, [numerical]{.alert}, and [ordinal]{.alert} variables - Distinguish [explanatory]{.alert} and [response]{.alert} variables ## What is a [variable]{.alert}? > [Variables]{.alert} are characteristics that could differ among individuals or other sampling units ## What is a [variable]{.alert}? [Categorical]{.alert} data are qualitative characteristics of individuals that do not have magnitude on a numerical scale
[Numerical]{.alert} data are quantitative measurements that have magnitude on a numerical scale
[Ordinal]{.alert} data are qualitative measurements, but ordered ## [Explanatory]{.alert} vs. [Response]{.alert} variables Variables can be either [explanatory]{.alert} or [response]{.alert} variables
[Explanatory]{.alert} variables are hypothesized to cause, directly or indirectly, a change in a [response]{.alert} variable ## [Explanatory]{.alert} vs. [Response]{.alert} variables Typical notation: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Symbol |Variable | |:----------|:-----------------------------------------------------------| |$Y$ |Response | |$X$ |Explanatory (e.g. $Y = \beta_X X$) | |$X_1, X_2$ |Multiple explanatory (e.g. $Y = \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2$) | ::: :::
Just because a statistical model says $X$ "causes" $Y$, it doesn't necessarily mean it's true ## 3. Randomly sample a population **Learning goals:** - Know that a good sample is *precise* and *unbiased* - Distinguish the [precision]{.alert} and [bias]{.alert} of a sample - Know that a [random sample]{.alert} involves *equal chance* and *independence* - Identify sources of bias in a nonrandom sample ## Why sample? > We don't have time, budget, ability to measure every unit in a population ## Random and independent samples ::: {.pause-think} Recall the **uhu body sizes** activity 1. If we treat all the "uhu" scattered around the classroom as the [population]{.alert} and the data collected by each of the 5 sections as 5 [samples]{.alert}, are the samples [random]{.alert}? 2. Are the samples [independent]{.alert}? 3. What types of processes or mistakes could lead to non-random and/or non-independent samples? ::: ## Why do we care? Whether or not samples are [random]{.alert} and [independent]{.alert} impacts our [estimates]{.alert} ::: {.fragment} That happens due to: - Inaccurate assessment of uncertainty: non-random and non-independent samples artificially decrease uncertainty - Change in precision - Change in bias ::: ## Why do we care? [Precision]{.alert} and [bias]{.alert} ![](/img/ws1-2-2.jpg){width="65%" fig-align="center"} ## Obtaining good samples ::: {.incremental} - Decreasing variance increases precision - Reduced measurement error - Large samples increase precision - Reduced sampling error - But very precise measurement and large samples can still be biased! - In fact, large sample size reinforces bias - Random sampling leads to unbiased estimates ::: ## [Random]{.alert} samples A sample is random if two criteria are met: ::: {.incremental} 1. Every unit in the population has an [equal chance]{.alert} of being sampled 2. The probability that one unit is sampled is [independent]{.alert} of another unit being sampled ::: ## [Random]{.alert} samples ::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.pause-think} Suppose you are running a clinical study to document the effect of noni on arthritis care. Your treatments are `YES noni` and `NO noni`. You allow participants to choose their treatment and to switch between treatments such that some of the data points in the `YES noni` and `NO noni` treatments come from the same people ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} :::: {.r-stack} ::::: {.fragment .fade-out} ![](/img/noni.jpg){width="90%"} ::::: ::::: {.fragment} 1. Are these samples random and independent? Why or why not? 2. If not, what could be the statistical problems you encounter? 3. If not, how would you fix the study design? ::::: :::: ::: ::: ## [Indigenous knowledge]{.alert} ::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.pause-think} Noni is a kupuna crop. The ʻike of its uses come from inter-generational kilo by Kānaka ʻŌiwi. - Who gets to benefit from production of noni as commodity? - Who gets to decide to commodify/how to commodify noni to begin with? ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.r-stack} ```{=html}
